title: Devilled Kidneys
subtitle: Lamb kidneys on toast with a hot mustard and cayenne sauce
excerpt: Lamb kidneys cooked fast in butter with English mustard, Worcestershire sauce, and cayenne, served on hot buttered toast. A Victorian-era British breakfast or savoury that is faster and better than it sounds to most people.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136. Devilled kidneys listed as a breakfast or savoury dish. Eliza Acton, Modern Cookery for Private Families (1845), kidneys as a standard breakfast item. Devilled kidneys were served at Victorian and Edwardian breakfast sideboards and have been part of the full English tradition since at least 1850.

content.text: Devilled kidneys are halved lamb kidneys cooked fast in a very hot pan with butter and a pungent sauce of English mustard, Worcestershire sauce, and cayenne, then put on hot buttered toast. The kidneys must be cooked on high heat and served immediately: they are quick to cook and toughen if left too long. Halved and the cores removed, they are less fearsome than the name suggests.

items.prepNote: halved and cores removed with scissors
a small handful, roughly chopped, to serve

content.text: Mix {{english-mustard}} of English mustard, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce, {{cayenne-pepper}} of cayenne, and juice of {{lemon}} in a small bowl. Set aside.
Toast {{bread-white}} bread and butter the slices with {{salted-butter}} of salted butter. Keep warm.
Heat a frying pan over high heat until very hot. Add {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and, once it foams, add {{lamb-kidneys}} halved kidneys, cut-side down. Cook for 2 minutes, then flip.
After 1 minute on the second side, pour in the devil sauce and toss to coat. Cook for 30 seconds more until the sauce is glossy and just reduced. The kidneys should be just pink in the centre.
Spoon onto the buttered toast. Scatter parsley over the top and serve immediately.

rows.symptom: Kidneys are grey and rubbery all the way through
rows.fix: Kidneys should be pink in the centre: 2 minutes on one side, 1 minute on the other, then 30 seconds in the sauce. Remove from the heat the moment the sauce glosses.

rows.symptom: Kidneys have a strong, unpleasant smell
rows.fix: Cut each kidney in half and use scissors to snip out the white core and any tubes. Rinse briefly in cold water and pat dry.

rows.cause: Pan not hot enough when sauce was added, or too much liquid
rows.fix: Add the sauce to a very hot pan. It will reduce rapidly. If still thin, remove the kidneys and boil the sauce for 30 seconds.

rows.symptom: Toast is soggy before the kidneys are cooked
rows.fix: Make the toast while the kidneys cook, not before. Butter and keep in the oven at low heat if needed.

content.text: Devilled kidneys were a standard breakfast dish in Victorian and Edwardian households. They were kept warm in chafing dishes on the breakfast sideboard. The devilling technique, using mustard, cayenne, and strong sauces, was a common way to treat offal and leftover meat. The dish fell from fashion as offal consumption declined in Britain. It is now found in traditional British restaurants and country house hotels.
